title: Struct Initialization and Aggregate Values
learningObjectives: Explain initialization order and member mapping.
Use value initialization to avoid indeterminate fields.
Initialize arrays of structured objects safely.

understand.concept: Aggregate initialization fills members in declaration order with brace values. Omitted aggregate members can be initialized from defaults or value-initialized depending on the form.
understand.whyItMatters: Clear initialization reduces uninitialized data and makes object creation readable.
understand.explain: Keep initializer order aligned with member declaration; use braces and explicit defaults.

examples.title: Brace initialization
examples.explanation: Values initialize members in declaration order.

examples.title: Value initialize
examples.explanation: Empty braces value-initialize members (false for bool).

examples.title: Partial aggregate
examples.explanation: The omitted amount is value-initialized to zero.

examples.title: Initialize array of structs
examples.explanation: Each array element is initialized with its own aggregate.

practise.guidedTask: For Struct Initialization and Aggregate Values, trace every example. List each type, object, member, initial value, access path, and state change. Identify where encapsulation or initialization affects correctness.
practise.independentTask: Create a small C++ model focused on Struct Initialization and Aggregate Values (such as a Point, Student, Product, or Account). Include multiple objects, initialization, at least one operation/member access, and test normal, boundary and invalid states. Explain which fields should be public or private and why.
hints: Define the type and its responsibilities before creating objects.
Initialize members deliberately and trace their values.
Use dot for objects and arrow only for pointers.
Keep fields private when they must enforce rules.
Test object creation, valid operations and rejected updates.

questions.explanation: Value initialization gives zero/false defaults for these simple types.
Default member initializers provide a starting value.
